title: Bash Startup Files
subtitle: Which files Bash reads — by interactive vs login — flip to reveal meaning

cards.meaning: Scripts Bash reads and executes when it starts; which ones depend on how the shell was started
cards.notes: Not which machine — interactive? and login?

cards.meaning: You can type commands; the shell is not running only because a script launched it
Shell after authenticating (SSH, TTY/console), or Bash started with bash --login / bash -l
cards.notes: Follows the profile-file path

cards.meaning: /etc/profile, then first readable of ~/.bash_profile ~/.bash_login ~/.profile; on logout ~/.bash_logout
cards.notes: Memory: login = profile family

cards.meaning: ~/.bashrc only
cards.example: Terminal icon/menu on a graphical desktop
cards.notes: Memory: non-login = rc only. /etc/profile and profile trio are not read

cards.meaning: System-wide; runs for every login shell on the box
cards.notes: First file in the login path

cards.meaning: First of the personal login trio tried; if readable, ~/.bash_login and ~/.profile are skipped
cards.notes: Only one of the three personal files is read

cards.meaning: Second personal login-file candidate; used only if ~/.bash_profile is missing/unreadable
cards.notes: Tried after ~/.bash_profile, before ~/.profile

cards.meaning: Third personal login-file candidate; used only if the first two are missing/unreadable
cards.notes: Often portable; prefer . (dot) over source here

cards.meaning: Per-user; runs when that login shell exits
cards.notes: Logout has its own file

cards.meaning: Per-user file for interactive non-login shells: aliases, functions, PS1, umask for that window, completion
cards.notes: rc = run commands for this interactive session

cards.meaning: ~/.bash_profile, then ~/.bash_login, then ~/.profile — only the first existing readable one runs
cards.notes: If ~/.bash_profile exists and is readable, the other two are skipped

cards.meaning: PATH, umask, environment variables that child processes should inherit
Start a login shell as you — reads your profile files; no password, no user switch, not root
cards.notes: Same as bash -l. Use to test /etc/profile and ~/.bash_profile without a new SSH

cards.meaning: Same as bash --login — login shell as you
Substitute user — switch to another account (default root); needs that user’s password; changes UID
cards.notes: Not a startup-file switch. Job is become root (or su user)

cards.meaning: Still switch to root; - gives root a clean login environment (their home, their PATH)
cards.notes: Same as su -l. Without - you still become root but keep more of your env and cwd

cards.meaning: Switch to that named user (their password)
Switch to that user with their login environment
su becomes root/other UID (password); bash --login starts a login shell as you (your profile files, no password)
cards.notes: Do not treat them as two login-shell commands

cards.meaning: Login shells do not read ~/.bashrc alone; GUI terminals often skip ~/.bash_profile — one file sources the other so aliases and PATH both apply
cards.notes: Door (.bash_profile) should open onto the furnished room (.bashrc)

cards.meaning: Runs the file in the current shell (not a subshell), so export, aliases, and functions stay
cards.notes: “Referred to” means sourced, not merely mentioned

cards.meaning: POSIX: read and run a file in the current shell; required in sh
cards.notes: Need a space: . ~/.bashrc. Prefer . in ~/.profile, /etc/profile, portable scripts

cards.meaning: Same effect as . in Bash, but Bash-specific — not required by POSIX; dash/sh may say source: not found
cards.notes: Fine in Bash-only files; use . for portability

cards.meaning: Portable Operating System Interface (IEEE Std 1003) — shared Unix contract for shell language, utilities, and C APIs
cards.notes: Bash = POSIX plus extras. /bin/sh is often dash, not Bash

cards.meaning: The POSIX shell on the box — on many Linux systems dash, not Bash, so Bash extras are missing
Current shell name; a leading - often means login (e.g. -bash)
Prints on or off — whether this is a login shell
